claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
In the past, having more choices usually meant more complexity, which added technical debt and meant hours of setup.
GeoDeploy (github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy) takes a container image and user geo locations and determines where it should run and what it will cost, then builds the deployment.

A GeoDeploy deployment request consists of four parts: target geos (traffic share and data-residency rule: EU-only, US-only, or in-country), an image with platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max provider count, budget).
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, and does all the math but never makes judgment calls; Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use but never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS but decides nothing.
GeoDeploy's first pipeline step maps each business region (geo) to a canonical location and residency class.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate.
GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run provisioning unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The Pulumi Automation API link points to /automation/.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric you describe; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets in GeoDeploy, so a hallucinated region such as us-west-9 or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction; Jev never writes code or does arithmetic.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates, along with the constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

GeoDeploy asks Jev for one selection (choice), five quality scores (coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks via noul (data residency satisfied, enough capacity), and a fallback choice of backup region.
GeoDeploy's packages/decide/src/questions.ts contains buildStageAQuestions, which imports choice, noul, score from "@typesafe-ai/sdk".
TypeSafe advises to "describe situations, not degrees" when writing rubrics.

GeoDeploy's rubrics use 10 levels, each a concrete scenario, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
The options passed to choice() are the priced candidates keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.

The TypeSafe SDK provides a TypeSafeClient with a systemOne method taking state and questions, returning answers with fields such as selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking uses weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because the weights live in code, GeoDeploy's ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profiles: latency-optimized {cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12}; balanced {0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.12, 0.18}; residency-first {0.12, 0.12, 0.38, 0.23, 0.15}; failure-domain {0.08, 0.17, 0.48, 0.15, 0.12}.
In GeoDeploy's composite score, sprawl risk is subtracted, because every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence gate thresholds: data residency 0.95 (hard reject); region for new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human choice); region when stack exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (use registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (use bin-packing result); region pick, residency, or capacity global floor 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
GeoDeploy's residency check in packages/decide/src/engine.ts hard-rejects (throws AiPathAborted) when residencyOk confidence is below 0.95 and when the selection is not one of the candidates.
Each AiPathAborted in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream is unreachable, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

Self-driving mode is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`; the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.
In self-driving mode, code, not Jev, computes the actual node-count changes.

In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency and error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
GeoDeploy is released as open source, and getting started requires access to Jev and a cloud provider.
The GitHub repository pulumi/devx-geodeploy exists.
Pulumi's X account is @PulumiCorp.

GeoDeploy picks the best AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud region for users, gates every AI decision on confidence, provisions Kubernetes with one Pulumi stack per region, and scales itself in self-driving mode with a human in the loop when confidence is low.
GeoDeploy is open source.
